performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
question: Can the distance between two notes identify a pair as clearly as its tone colour?
intro: Five instrumental pairs keep five different distances between their notes. A brass chorale interrupts the procession before the pairs return with new companions.

sections.label: Drum introduction
sections.mNote: a short side-drum pattern prepares the procession

sections.label: Five pairs
sections.mNote: bassoons, oboes, clarinets, flutes and muted trumpets introduce separate ideas

sections.label: Brass chorale
sections.mNote: sustained brass replaces the paired procession

sections.label: Pairs with companions
sections.mNote: the earlier sequence returns with enriched accompaniment

sections.label: Closing assembly
sections.mNote: the groups converge before the drum has the last word

cues.title: A drum without snares
cues.text: The side drum begins alone, with its snares disengaged. Its dry pattern acts as a frame for the paired wind music rather than an accompaniment that must run throughout.
cues.evidence: Score p. 29, bars 1–7, explicitly “without snares”: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The cached report begins quietly and marks the first strong change at 0:12, the approximate start of the bassoon passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A new distance between voices
cues.text: The oboe pair follows the bassoons with a different interval between its two lines. Bassoons have sixths; oboes have thirds. The change concerns the shape of the duet as well as its colour.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 29–30, bassoons from bar 8 and oboes from bar 25: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Interval design corroborated at https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto. Novelty peaks at 0:12 and 0:32 anchor the approximate pair changes; the report does not measure two separate pitches.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A collector’s precise ear
cues.text: Bartók’s study of folk music continued after emigration, through work on South Slavic collections at Columbia University. His attention to small melodic and rhythmic differences belonged to that scholarly work as well as his composing.
cues.evidence: Rodda’s biographical account: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. This does not claim that any particular tune in this movement is a collected folk song.

cues.title: Five kinds of duet
cues.text: The five pairs do not share one melody. Their characteristic distances are sixths, thirds, sevenths, fifths and seconds. Listen for how close or widely spaced the voices seem, without needing to name every interval.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 29–35: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf; the five independent sections and their intervals are described at https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto. This surveys the whole procession; it does not assert that all five pairs sound at 1:45.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Jesting within the concerto
cues.text: Bartók described the concerto’s broader progress from sternness through the Elegia’s “death-song” towards the finale’s affirmation. He expressly excepted this second movement, calling it a jesting scherzo.
cues.evidence: Bartók’s programme note quoted by Rodda: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. A description of the cycle’s design, not a claim about Bartók’s private emotions during this passage.

cues.title: The procession becomes a chorale
cues.text: The centre exchanges separate wind duets for sustained brass harmony. The drum pattern remains a link with the surrounding music, so the change of manner is strong without being a complete change of world.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 36–37, brass chorale and side drum: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. From about 2:40 to 3:30 the report shows sustained level with lower brightness and much lower onset activity; the chorale boundary is estimated at the 2:38 novelty peak.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Preparing to move again
cues.text: Listen through the chorale’s withdrawal for the return of shorter, more mobile phrases. The pairs will recover their identities, but their surroundings will no longer be quite as spare.
cues.evidence: Score p. 37 into p. 38, return from bar 164: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Relative level drops to −28.4 dB at 3:35 before onset activity increases at 3:40; strongest novelty peak at 3:36. No exact first bassoon note is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Reiner and his former teacher
cues.text: Reiner had studied with Bartók at the Liszt Academy in Budapest. Their connection preceded both this Pittsburgh recording and Reiner’s later Chicago career.
cues.evidence: Chicago Symphony Archives identifies Bartók as one of Reiner’s teachers at the Liszt Academy: https://chicagosymphony.org/inside-the-music/article/8311/125-moments-011-first-grammy-awards . Contextual placement only.

cues.title: Recognisable but less solitary
cues.text: In the reprise, try to retain the identity of a pair while hearing the extra lines around it. The returning material does not need a bare accompaniment in order to remain recognisable.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 38–45 shows the enriched reprise, beginning with a third bassoon around the original pair: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf; Bartók’s explanation is quoted at https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto. The audio report anchors the return near 3:36, not each accompanying entry.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: More weight near the end
cues.text: The later return carries more recorded weight than much of the first procession. Follow the individual moving lines through that fuller sound, rather than expecting a simple repeat at the same strength.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/bartok-concerto-orchestra-coppie.txt: levels around 5:00–5:30 stay near −14 to −13 dB, compared with many −20 to −25 dB windows in the first procession. This is a within-file level comparison, not a measure of how many players are active.

cues.title: The frame closes quietly
cues.text: The last sustained wind harmony dies away and the side drum completes its short pattern. The ending recalls the opening’s dry sound instead of seeking a large orchestral finish.
cues.evidence: Score p. 46, bars 252–263, sustained winds followed by exposed side drum without snares: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Reported level falls from −17.4 dB at 5:40 to −34.0 at 5:45; passage timing is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A dry pattern admits the bassoons
transitions.how: The side drum establishes a short rhythmic frame before two bassoons enter in parallel sixths. Pizzicato strings provide a light footing. The drum’s withdrawal leaves the duet exposed, so the first change is chiefly one of colour and foreground rather than a new pulse.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 29, bars 1–24: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty peak at 0:12; level rises from −24.4 dB at 0:10 to −17.7 at 0:15. Approximate passage boundary.

transitions.title: Separate voices give way to harmony
transitions.how: After the five contrasting duets, a sustained brass chorale replaces the more articulated procession. The side drum links this broader texture with the opening. A change in duration and orchestral grouping makes the new section distinct without requiring a general pause.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 35–37: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty peak at 2:38; onset rate falls from 6.4/s at 2:30 to 0.8/s at 2:40. The score, not spectral measurement, identifies brass and drum.

transitions.title: The pairs return with company
transitions.how: The brass harmony subsides and the bassoon duet returns. A third bassoon now moves around the original pair; subsequent groups also gain new companions. This is a recognisable return whose accompaniment changes its texture, rather than an exact replay of the first procession.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 37–38, bars 164 onward: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Strongest novelty peak at 3:36, with a quiet trough at 3:35 and renewed onset activity at 3:40. Passage alignment, not bar-exact synchronisation.

transitions.title: The many pairs gather and recede
transitions.how: The enriched procession converges in a short closing assembly. Sustained wind harmony outlasts the moving string figures, then the dry side-drum pattern is left exposed. The movement closes its own frame by subtraction, not by adding a final loud tutti.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 46, bars 248–263: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty peaks at 5:30 and 5:34 precede the marked level fall at 5:45. The 5:30 anchor covers the whole closing passage, not the drum’s first isolated stroke.

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, II
source.locator: Printed pp. 29–46. Scored passage snapshots, approximately placed using novelty at 12, 32, 76, 158, 216 and 330 seconds; intervening pair entries are proportioned, with roughly 10-second tolerance. The stage does not infer instruments from the mono spectrum.

timeline.note: Two bassoons in sixths above light pizzicato accompaniment (p. 29).
Oboes in thirds; strings alternate plucked and bowed figures, with brief drum punctuation (p. 30).
The clarinet pair occupies the next slot in the procession, in sevenths (pp. 30–32).
Flutes in fifths replace the clarinet foreground (pp. 32–34).
Muted trumpets in seconds conclude the first sequence; strings provide mobile accompaniment (pp. 34–35).
The brass chorale is accompanied by the side-drum pattern (pp. 36–37).
The returning bassoon pair gains a third bassoon’s winding accompaniment (pp. 37–38).
The oboe return is reinforced by clarinets, amid a more elaborate accompaniment (p. 39).
The closing assembly gives way to sustained wind harmony and the drum (p. 46); this snapshot spans the successive thinning, not continuous tutti.
The side drum completes the frame after the sustained wind sound recedes (p. 46).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: A pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.
facts: Budapest Academy of Music, 1899–1903: piano with István Thomán, composition with Hans Koessler
Piano professor, Budapest Academy, 1907–34 · Hungarian Academy of Sciences folk-music project, 1934–40 · Columbia University research in American exile
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages · Biskra, Algeria, 1913 · Turkey, 1936
Six string quartets · three piano concertos · two violin concertos · three stage works · folk-music collections and pedagogical music
composer.background:
Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós, a town in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary which became part of Romania after the First World War. His father, who directed an agricultural school, died in 1888; his mother, Paula Voit, supported Béla and his sister by teaching. After several moves the family settled in Pozsony, now Bratislava. The changing names on this map matter: the Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian communities he later recorded occupied overlapping musical territories. His professional education began within the German-speaking conservatoire tradition.

At the Budapest Academy from 1899 to 1903, he studied piano with István Thomán, a pupil of Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler. Hearing Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra in 1902 helped release him from student exercises. Kossuth, composed in 1903, made the Hungarian revolutionary leader the subject of a large orchestral narrative and caricatured Haydn’s imperial anthem as the Austrian enemy. This early nationalist programme preceded the comparative research that would complicate his understanding of national music.
